script.title: A Confident AI Answer Can Still Be Wrong
script.description: NIST calls confidently false generated content confabulation. This explainer separates fluent answers from verified evidence.
script.topic: A Confident AI Answer Can Still Be Wrong
script.why_us: US-focused educational explanation from reviewed primary sources.
script.timely_basis: Dated historical evidence or evergreen explanation; no claim of a current trend.

scenes.narration: An AI answer can sound certain and still be false; NIST describes this risk as confabulation.
Fluent wording and factual support are different properties, so confidence in the writing does not establish accuracy.

diagram.title: Confidence is not evidence
diagram.note: A convincing answer can still contain errors.

scenes.narration: A generated answer may also include inaccurate references, which makes checking the underlying documents important rather than optional.
Google likewise warns that generative systems can produce inaccurate or unexpected outputs, even when the requested task sounds straightforward.
Connecting an answer to source material can improve factuality, but the output still needs evaluation for the actual application.
The practical distinction is simple: an answer is generated text; reliable evidence comes from checking what supports its claims.

diagram.title: Separate answer from evidence
diagram.note: Source checks help manage errors; they do not promise perfection.

sources.title: Reviewed primary-source evidence
sources.content: NIST AI 600-1, July 2024, identifies confabulation: generative AI can confidently present erroneous or false content. Outputs can contain inaccurate information or false citations. Confident language is not proof of accuracy. Evaluation and verification of generated content are part of managing the risk; no model output should be treated as inherently verified.

sources.title: Reviewed primary-source evidence
sources.content: Generative AI can produce inaccurate or unexpected outputs. Post-processing and rigorous manual evaluation are important. Grounding with Google Search can improve factuality by connecting output to source information; it does not establish that every output is correct. Developers must evaluate applications rather than assume all generated output is reliable.
